{{Short description|Representation of water movement in unsaturated soils}}
The '''Richards equation''' represents the movement of water in [[Vadose zone|unsaturated]] soils, and is attributed to [[Lorenzo A. Richards]] who published the equation in 1931.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal|author=Richards, L.A. |year=1931 |title=Capillary conduction of liquids through porous mediums |journal=Physics |volume=1 |issue=5 |pages=318–333 |doi=10.1063/1.1745010 |bibcode = 1931Physi...1..318R}}</ref> It is a [[Differential equation|quasilinear]] [[partial differential equation]]; its analytical solution is often limited to specific initial and boundary conditions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Tracy |first=F. T. |date=August 2006 |title=Clean two- and three-dimensional analytical solutions of Richards' equation for testing numerical solvers: TECHNICAL NOTE |journal=Water Resources Research |language=en |volume=42 |issue=8 |doi=10.1029/2005WR004638|s2cid=119938184 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Proof of the [[Existence theorem|existence]] and [[Uniqueness theorem|uniqueness]] of solution was given only in 1983 by [[Hans Wilhelm Alt|Alt]] and [[Stephan Luckhaus|Luckhaus]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wilhelm Alt |first1=Hans |last2=Luckhaus |first2=Stephan |date=1 September 1983|title=Quasilinear elliptic-parabolic differential equations |journal=Mathematische Zeitschrift |language=en |volume=183 |issue=3 |pages=311–341 |doi=10.1007/BF01176474 |s2cid=120607569 |issn=1432-1823}}</ref>  The equation is based on Darcy-Buckingham law<ref name=":0" /> representing flow in porous media under variably saturated conditions, which is stated as

:<math>\vec{q}=-\mathbf{K}(\theta) (\nabla h + \nabla z),</math>
where 
:<math>\vec{q}</math> is the  [[volumetric flux]] [L/T];
:<math>\theta</math> is the  [[Water content|volumetric water content]] [1];
:<math>h</math> is the liquid [[pressure head]], which is negative for unsaturated porous media [L];
:<math>\mathbf{K}(h)</math> is the unsaturated [[hydraulic conductivity]] [L/T];
:<math>\nabla z</math> is the geodetic head gradient, which is assumed as <math>\nabla z = \left(\begin{smallmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{smallmatrix} \right)</math> for three-dimensional problems.

Richards equation is derived by first considering the law of [[mass conservation]] for an incompressible [[porous medium]] and constant liquid density, expressed as

:<math>\frac{\partial \theta}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \vec{q} + S = 0</math>,
where 
:<math>S</math> is the source/sink term [T<math>^{-1}</math>], typically root water uptake.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Feddes |first1=R. A. |last2=Zaradny |first2=H. |date=1 May 1978|title=Model for simulating soil-water content considering evapotranspiration — Comments |journal=Journal of Hydrology |language=en |volume=37 |issue=3 |pages=393–397 |doi=10.1016/0022-1694(78)90030-6 |bibcode=1978JHyd...37..393F |issn=0022-1694}}</ref> Then substituting the fluxes by the Darcy-Buckingham law the following mixed-form Richards equation is obtained:

:<math> \frac{\partial \theta}{\partial t} = \nabla \cdot \mathbf{K}(h) (\nabla h + \nabla z) - S </math>.

For modeling of one-dimensional infiltration this [[divergence]] form reduces to

:<math>\frac{\partial \theta}{\partial t}= \frac{\partial}{\partial z} 
\left( \mathbf{K}(\theta) \left (\frac{\partial h}{\partial z} + 1 \right) \right) - S </math>.

Although attributed to L. A. Richards, the equation was originally introduced 9 years earlier by [[Lewis Fry Richardson]] in 1922.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Knight|first1=John|last2=Raats|first2=Peter|title=The contributions of Lewis Fry Richardson to drainage theory, soil physics, and the soil-plant-atmosphere continuum|url=http://meetingorganizer.copernicus.org/EGU2016/EGU2016-10980-1.pdf|publisher=EGU General Assembly 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Richardson|first1=Lewis Fry|title=Weather prediction by numerical process|date=1922|publisher=Cambridge, The University press|pages=[https://archive.org/details/weatherpredictio00richrich/page/n222 262]|url=https://archive.org/details/weatherpredictio00richrich}}</ref>

==Formulations==
The Richards equation appears in many articles in the environmental literature because it describes the flow in the [[vadose zone]] between the atmosphere and the [[aquifer]]. It also appears in pure mathematical journals because it has non-trivial solutions. The above-given mixed formulation involves two unknown variables: <math>\theta</math> and <math>h</math>. This can be easily resolved by considering constitutive relation <math>\theta(h)</math>, which is known as the [[water retention curve]]. Applying the [[chain rule]], the Richards equation may be reformulated as either <math>h</math>-form (head based) or <math>\theta</math>-form (saturation based) Richards equation.

===Head-based===
By applying the [[chain rule]] on temporal derivative leads to 
: <math>\frac{\partial \theta(h)}{\partial t} = \frac{\textrm{d} \theta}{\textrm{d} h} \frac{\partial h}{\partial t} </math>,
where  <math>\frac{\textrm{d} \theta}{\textrm{d} h}</math> is known as the [[retention water capacity]] <math> C(h) </math>. The equation is then stated as
:<math> C(h)\frac{\partial h}{\partial t}= \nabla \cdot \left( \mathbf{K}(h) \nabla h + \nabla z\right) - S </math>.

The head-based Richards equation is prone to the following computational issue: the discretized temporal derivative using the implicit [[Erich Rothe|Rothe]] method yields the following approximation:

<math>\frac{\Delta \theta}{\Delta t} \approx C(h) \frac{\Delta h}{\Delta t}, \quad \mbox{and so}  \quad \frac{\Delta \theta}{\Delta t} - C(h) \frac{\Delta h}{\Delta t} = \varepsilon .</math>

This approximation produces an error <math>\varepsilon</math> that affects the mass conservation of the numerical solution, and so special strategies for temporal derivatives treatment are necessary.<ref>{{Cite journal|author1-link=Michael A. Celia |last1=Celia |first1=Michael A. |last2=Bouloutas |first2=Efthimios T. |last3=Zarba |first3=Rebecca L. |date=July 1990 |title=A general mass-conservative numerical solution for the unsaturated flow equation |url=http://doi.wiley.com/10.1029/WR026i007p01483 |journal=Water Resources Research |language=en |volume=26 |issue=7 |pages=1483–1496 |doi=10.1029/WR026i007p01483|bibcode=1990WRR....26.1483C |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

===Saturation-based===
By applying the [[chain rule]] on the spatial derivative leads to
:<math> \mathbf{K}(h) \nabla h = \mathbf{K}(h) \frac{\textrm{d}h}{\textrm{d} \theta} \nabla \theta, </math>
where <math>\mathbf{K}(h) \frac{\textrm{d}h}{\textrm{d} \theta}</math>, which could be further formulated as <math>\frac{\mathbf{K}(\theta)}{C(\theta)}</math>, is known as the [[soil water diffusivity]] <math>\mathbf{D}(\theta)</math>. The equation is then stated as

:<math> \frac{\partial \theta }{\partial t}= \nabla \cdot \mathbf{D}(\theta) \nabla \theta - S. </math>

The saturation-based Richards equation is prone to the following computational issues. Since the limits <math> \lim_{\theta \to \theta_s} ||\mathbf{D}(\theta)|| = \infty </math> and <math>\lim_{\theta \to \theta_r}||\mathbf{D}(\theta)|| = \infty</math>, where <math> \theta_s </math> is the saturated (maximal) water content and <math>\theta_r</math> is the residual (minimal) water content a successful numerical solution is restricted just for ranges of water content satisfactory below the full saturation (the saturation should be even lower than [[Water retention curve|air entry value]]) as well as satisfactory above the residual water content.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kuráž |first1=Michal |last2=Mayer |first2=Petr |last3=Lepš |first3=Matěj |last4=Trpkošová |first4=Dagmar |date=2010-04-15 |title=An adaptive time discretization of the classical and the dual porosity model of Richards' equation |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0377042709008036 |journal=Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics |series=Finite Element Methods in Engineering and Science (FEMTEC 2009) |language=en |volume=233 |issue=12 |pages=3167–3177 |doi=10.1016/j.cam.2009.11.056 |bibcode=2010JCoAM.233.3167K |issn=0377-0427|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Parametrization==
The Richards equation in any of its forms involves soil hydraulic properties, which is a set of five parameters representing [[soil type]]. The soil hydraulic properties typically consist of [[water retention curve]] parameters by van Genuchten:<ref>{{Cite journal |last=van Genuchten |first=M. Th. |date=September 1980|title=A Closed-form Equation for Predicting the Hydraulic Conductivity of Unsaturated Soils |url=http://doi.wiley.com/10.2136/sssaj1980.03615995004400050002x |journal=Soil Science Society of America Journal |language=en |volume=44 |issue=5 |pages=892–898 |doi=10.2136/sssaj1980.03615995004400050002x|bibcode=1980SSASJ..44..892V |url-access=subscription }}</ref> (<math> \alpha, \, n, \,m, \, \theta_s, \theta_r </math>), where <math>\alpha</math> is the inverse of air entry value  [L<sup>−1</sup>], <math>n</math> is the pore size distribution parameter [-], and <math>m</math> is usually assumed as  <math>m= 1-\frac{1}{n}</math>. Further the saturated hydraulic conductivity <math>\mathbf{K}_s</math> (which is for non [[Isotropy|isotropic]] environment a [[tensor]] of second order) should also be provided. Identification of these parameters is often non-trivial and was a subject of numerous publications over several decades.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Inoue |first1=M. |last2=Šimůnek |first2=J. |last3=Shiozawa |first3=S. |last4=Hopmans |first4=J.W. |date=June 2000|title=Simultaneous estimation of soil hydraulic and solute transport parameters from transient infiltration experiments |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0309170800000117 |journal=Advances in Water Resources |language=en |volume=23 |issue=7 |pages=677–688 |doi=10.1016/S0309-1708(00)00011-7|bibcode=2000AdWR...23..677I |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fodor |first1=Nándor |last2=Sándor |first2=Renáta |last3=Orfanus |first3=Tomas |last4=Lichner |first4=Lubomir |last5=Rajkai |first5=Kálmán |date=October 2011|title=Evaluation method dependency of measured saturated hydraulic conductivity |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0016706111001935 |journal=Geoderma |language=en |volume=165 |issue=1 |pages=60–68 |doi=10.1016/j.geoderma.2011.07.004|bibcode=2011Geode.165...60F |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Angulo-Jaramillo |first1=Rafael |last2=Vandervaere |first2=Jean-Pierre |last3=Roulier |first3=Stéphanie |last4=Thony |first4=Jean-Louis |last5=Gaudet |first5=Jean-Paul |last6=Vauclin |first6=Michel |date=May 2000|title=Field measurement of soil surface hydraulic properties by disc and ring infiltrometers |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0167198700000982 |journal=Soil and Tillage Research |language=en |volume=55 |issue=1–2 |pages=1–29 |doi=10.1016/S0167-1987(00)00098-2|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Köhne |first1=J. Maximilian |last2=Mohanty |first2=Binayak P. |last3=Šimůnek |first3=Jirka |date=January 2006|title=Inverse Dual-Permeability Modeling of Preferential Water Flow in a Soil Column and Implications for Field-Scale Solute Transport |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2136/vzj2005.0008 |journal=Vadose Zone Journal |language=en |volume=5 |issue=1 |pages=59–76 |doi=10.2136/vzj2005.0008 |bibcode=2006VZJ.....5...59K |s2cid=781417 |issn=1539-1663|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Younes |first1=Anis |last2=Mara |first2=Thierry |last3=Fahs |first3=Marwan |last4=Grunberger |first4=Olivier |last5=Ackerer |first5=Philippe |date=3 May 2017|title=Hydraulic and transport parameter assessment using column infiltration experiments |url=https://hess.copernicus.org/articles/21/2263/2017/ |journal=Hydrology and Earth System Sciences |language=en |volume=21 |issue=5 |pages=2263–2275 |doi=10.5194/hess-21-2263-2017 |bibcode=2017HESS...21.2263Y |issn=1607-7938|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kuraz |first1=Michal |last2=Jačka |first2=Lukáš |last3=Ruth Blöcher |first3=Johanna |last4=Lepš |first4=Matěj |date=1 November 2022|title=Automated calibration methodology to avoid convergence issues during inverse identification of soil hydraulic properties |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S096599782200179X |journal=Advances in Engineering Software |language=en |volume=173 |article-number=103278 |doi=10.1016/j.advengsoft.2022.103278 |s2cid=252508220 |issn=0965-9978|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Limitations==
The numerical solution of the Richards equation is one of the most challenging problems in earth science.<ref>Farthing, Matthew W., and Fred L. Ogden, (2017). Numerical solution of Richards' Equation: a review of advances and challenges. ''Soil Science Society of America Journal'', 81(6), pp.1257-1269.</ref> Richards' equation has been criticized for being computationally expensive and unpredictable <ref>Short, D., W.R. Dawes, and I. White, (1995).  The practicability of using Richards' equation for general purpose soil-water dynamics models.   ''Envir. Int'l''. 21(5):723-730.</ref><ref>Tocci, M. D., C. T. Kelley, and C. T. Miller (1997), Accurate and economical solution of the pressure-head form of Richards' equation by the method of lines, ''Adv. Wat. Resour.'', 20(1), 1–14.</ref> because there is no guarantee that a solver will converge for a particular set of soil constitutive relations.  Advanced computational and software solutions are required here to over-come this obstacle. The method has also been criticized for over-emphasizing the role of capillarity,<ref>Germann, P. (2010), Comment on "Theory for source-responsive and free-surface film modeling of unsaturated flow", ''Vadose Zone J.'' 9(4), 1000-1101.</ref> and for being in some ways 'overly simplistic' <ref>Gray, W. G., and S. Hassanizadeh (1991), Paradoxes and realities in unsaturated flow theory, ''Water Resour. Res.'', 27(8), 1847-1854.</ref>  In one dimensional simulations of rainfall infiltration into dry soils, fine spatial [[discretization]] less than one cm is required near the land surface,<ref>Downer, Charles W., and Fred L. Ogden (2003), ''Hydrol. Proc.'',18, pp. 1-22.  DOI:10.1002/hyp.1306.</ref> which is due to the small size of the [[representative elementary volume]] for [[multiphase flow]] in porous media.  In three-dimensional applications the numerical solution of the Richards equation is subject to [[aspect ratio]] constraints where the ratio of horizontal to vertical resolution in the solution domain should be less than about 7.{{citation needed|date=November 2022}}
